spine_heading: Malting is tricking the grain into digesting itself

sentences.text: The European and Middle Eastern answer uses the grain's own machinery.
A resting barley grain already holds one starch-cutting enzyme, beta-amylase, in an inactive form.
Germination wakes that one and produces the enzymes that will break the grain's starch down.
Let it sprout until the enzymes peak.
Then kiln it, which dries the grain and halts the germination.
The maltster's whole trick is to allow the sprouting and then stop it.
What the maltster is harvesting is enzymes, not flavour.
Flavour and colour arrive in the kiln instead, through the Maillard reaction.
Then a brewer or a distiller picks a mash temperature, and that choice is a dial with a predictable output.
Alpha-amylase peaks between sixty-three and seventy degrees Celsius.
Beta-amylase peaks lower, between fifty-five and sixty-five.
The two bands nearly overlap, so a single rest usually runs both enzymes at once.
Where inside that window the rest sits decides how much of the sugar the yeast can eat.
Rest hot and alpha-amylase leaves more sugar the yeast cannot use, so the drink finishes fuller and sweeter.
Rest cool instead and the same grain finishes thinner and drier.
That is a production step behaving like a dial rather than a ritual.

claims.text: Malting is steeping, germinating and drying grain; the enzymes produced during germination are what break the starch down for the brewer or distiller, and the maltster stops germination when the required enzymes are optimal.

sources.quote: Malting is the process of steeping, germinating, and drying grain to convert it into malt.
Germination and sprouting involve a number of enzymes to produce the changes from seed to seedling and the malt producer stops this stage of the process when the required enzymes are optimal.
The enzymes produced during germination are needed to break down the starch for the brewer or distiller during the mashing process.

claims.text: Beta-amylase is present in an inactive form prior to seed germination, and it acts on starch to produce maltose.

sources.quote: β-amylase is present in an inactive form prior to seed germination.
This enzyme acts on starch, glycogen and related polysaccharides and oligosaccharides producing beta-maltose by an inversion.

claims.text: Kilning reduces the grain's moisture content and stops the germination process.

sources.quote: Kilning reduces the grain moisture content and stops the germination process.

claims.text: The high temperatures of kilning produce the colour in the malt through the Maillard reaction.

sources.quote: The high temperatures of kilning also produce the colour in the malt through the Maillard reaction.

claims.text: Peak activity for alpha-amylase is 63-70 °C and for beta-amylase 55-65 °C, so the two rests are often performed at once, with the time and temperature of the rest determining the ratio of fermentable to non-fermentable sugars in the wort; a hotter rest gives a fuller-bodied, sweeter beer.
claims.tier_reason: quantitative — two temperature bands the listener is expected to retain

sources.quote: Because of the closeness in temperatures of peak activity of an α-amylase (63-70 °C) and β-amylase (55-65 °C), the two rests are often performed at once with the time and temperature of the rest determining the ratio of fermentable to non-fermentable sugars in the wort and, hence, the final sweetness of the fermented drink.
A hotter rest results in a fuller-bodied, sweeter beer as α-amylase produces more non-fermentable sugars.

claims.text: Mash temperature is a production step whose output is predictable from the setting, rather than a fixed traditional procedure.
claims.reasoning: C7.5 gives the causal mechanism — where the rest sits decides the sugar ratio and therefore the finished sweetness. C7.1 gives what makes the choice available at all: malting hands the brewer a stock of enzymes rather than a finished sugar. The characterisation of that as a dial rather than a ritual is the editorial point the beat exists to make, and it is recorded as an inference because no span states it.

claims.text: Alpha-amylase denatures above 78 °C, so the mash-out temperature rarely exceeds it and starch extracted above it cannot be broken down.
claims.not_spoken_reason: Cut by narration-craft §5d's cap of three numeric facts per narration item, not for relevance or for want of a source. Item T2-A already carries three (the four routes at C6.12, and the two temperature bands at C7.5). Kept in the record so the reference surface is complete and so a later item split can spend it. This is the concrete cost cited in narration-architecture.md §9.

sources.quote: Although mash temperature and viscosity are roughly inversely proportional, the ability of brewers and distillers to use this relationship is constrained by the fact that α-Amylase quickly denatures above 78 °C (172.4 °F). Any starches extracted once the mash is brought above this temperature cannot be broken down and will cause a starch haze in the finished product.
